lines.text: Close your eyes, and you could still pick this bottle out of a crowd. That was the whole point.
Coca-Cola started in eighteen eighty-six as a soda fountain drink. Five cents a glass. No bottle at all.
When bottlers took over, it shipped in plain, straight-sided glass with a paper label.
Those labels slid off in tubs of ice water, and copycats like Koka-Nola used the exact same bottles.
So in nineteen fifteen, the company asked for a bottle you could recognize by feel in the dark, or even broken on the ground.
At the Root Glass Company in Indiana, Earl Dean looked up coca and kola in an encyclopedia.
He found a cocoa pod instead. Wrong plant. Perfect shape. Its long ribs and round belly became the contour bottle.
The first version wobbled on the conveyor belt, so they slimmed it down. People called it the hobble skirt.
Painted labels arrived in nineteen fifty-seven. In nineteen sixty, the shape itself was trademarked.
Even the plastic bottles kept the curves.
So that shape isn't decoration. It's a hundred-year-old anti-copycat device you can feel.
